sentences.text: This part combines daytime minutes, the evening charge and customer-service calls and acts on 1296 of 4000 training customers, 305 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance of leaving is about 2% without it and about 8% with it.

Through it, daytime minutes add to the chance only above about 210 minutes (between 172 and 242 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: going from 0 to 271 minutes takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 39%.

Daytime minutes count much more with an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, in an uneven way: from about 3% to about 32% between 112 and 249 minutes, against about 3% to about 9% with a lower evening charge.
More customer-service calls take this addition away, in an uneven way: for the typical customer it acts on, from about 13% at 0 calls to about 3% at 3 calls.

This part adds up the state, the voice-mail plan, customer-service calls and some usage figures with fixed weights: a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 3% to about 1%, and each extra call to customer service adds about the same, from about 2% at 0 to about 5% at 3 calls.
More voice-mail messages, a higher night-time charge, a higher international charge, more international minutes and more daytime calls each raise it steadily by about a point.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3% in most other states to about 9% in California, about 8% in Washington and about 6% in Montana, and down to under 1% in Arkansas, Vermont and Hawaii (41 to 80 training customers per state; the full list is in the technical detail).

This part reads the international plan and the state and acts on 453 of 4000 training customers, 170 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 2% without it and about 63% with it.
An international plan takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 24%, and a customer in Connecticut from about 3% to about 62%.
Through this part, customer-service calls add only from about 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way: going from 0 to 4 calls takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 7%.
It acts on 848 of 4000 training customers, 215 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 6% without it and about 6% with it.

This part combines customer-service calls with low daytime use and acts on 1494 of 4000 training customers, 204 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 4% without it and about 5% with it.

summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 3%; it adds up eleven parts: the main ones are heavy day and evening use, fixed-weight inputs, the international plan, a service-call step and low daytime use with calls, and the rest are small state and usage units.

This part combines daytime minutes, the evening charge and customer-service calls and acts on 1296 of 4000 training customers, 305 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance of leaving is about 2% without it and about 8% with it.

Through it, daytime minutes add to the chance only above about 210 minutes (between 172 and 242 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: going from 0 to 271 minutes takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 39%.

Daytime minutes count much more with an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, in an uneven way: from about 3% to about 32% between 112 and 249 minutes, against about 3% to about 9% with a lower evening charge.
More customer-service calls take this addition away, in an uneven way: for the typical customer it acts on, from about 13% at 0 calls to about 3% at 3 calls.

This part adds up the state, the voice-mail plan, customer-service calls and some usage figures with fixed weights: a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 3% to about 1%, and each extra call to customer service adds about the same, from about 2% at 0 to about 5% at 3 calls.
More voice-mail messages, a higher night-time charge, a higher international charge, more international minutes and more daytime calls each raise it steadily by about a point.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3% in most other states to about 9% in California, about 8% in Washington and about 6% in Montana, and down to under 1% in Arkansas, Vermont and Hawaii (41 to 80 training customers per state; the full list is in the technical detail).

This part reads the international plan and the state and acts on 453 of 4000 training customers, 170 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 2% without it and about 63% with it.
An international plan takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 24%, and a customer in Connecticut from about 3% to about 62%.
Through this part, customer-service calls add only from about 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way: going from 0 to 4 calls takes a typical customer from about 3% to about 7%.
It acts on 848 of 4000 training customers, 215 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 6% without it and about 6% with it.

This part reads only the state: it lowers the chance for 3922 of 4000 training customers, from about 26% to about 3% for its typical customer, and through it a customer in Arkansas, where it does not act, has about 26% instead of about 3%.
Across the whole model a customer in Arkansas comes out at about 3%.

This part combines customer-service calls with low daytime use and acts on 1494 of 4000 training customers, 204 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 4% without it and about 5% with it.

Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance steadily up to about 149 minutes (between 126 and 197 minutes for different customers), then no further, from about 4% at 91 to about 3% at 352 minutes for a typical customer.

This part reads daytime minutes and the area code and acts on 223 of 4000 training customers, 133 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 66% without it and about 71% with it, and area code 408 takes it back to about 66%.
This part acts only on the 72 training customers in New Mexico, 9 of whom left, and lowers the chance for its typical customer from about 4% to about 3%; night-time calls barely change it.
This part reads only the state and acts on 3944 of 4000 training customers, lowering their chance by less than a point; through it, customers in Pennsylvania and Michigan have about 3%.
This part acts only on the 77 training customers in Mississippi, 13 of whom left, and changes their chance by less than a point.
Through this part, a customer in Delaware has the same chance as others, about 3%.

In the training data, 215 of these 848 customers had churn.

Through this part, the customer-service calls only slightly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 3 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 7%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
